questions.question: What is the time complexity of accessing an element by index in an array?
questions.explanation: Arrays sit in contiguous memory, so the address of index i is computed directly as base address plus i times element size. No searching is needed.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of searching for an element in an unsorted array of n elements?
questions.explanation: With no ordering to exploit, you may have to check every one of the n elements before you find, or rule out, the target.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of inserting an element at the beginning of an unsorted array?
questions.explanation: Every existing element has to shift one position to the right to make room at index 0, touching all n elements.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of a dynamic array over a fixed-size array?
answers: It can resize itself when full
questions.explanation: A dynamic array (like C#'s List) automatically allocates a bigger backing array and copies elements over when it fills up, so you never need to know the size in advance.

questions.question: What does bubble sort do during each pass through the array?
answers: Divides the array in half and sorts each half
Finds the minimum element and moves it to the front
Swaps adjacent elements that are out of order
Selects a pivot and partitions elements around it
questions.explanation: Bubble sort walks the array comparing neighbours and swapping any pair that is out of order, letting the largest unsorted value bubble to the end each pass.

questions.question: What is the best-case time complexity of insertion sort?
questions.explanation: If the array is already sorted, each element only needs one comparison against its neighbour before insertion sort confirms it is already in place, giving a single O(n) pass.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm always performs O(n^2) comparisons regardless of input order?
questions.explanation: Selection sort always scans the entire remaining unsorted section to find the minimum, doing the same number of comparisons whether the input is sorted, reversed, or random.

questions.question: What is the core idea behind merge sort?
answers: Pick a pivot and partition the array around it
Divide into halves, then merge the sorted halves
Find the minimum and move it to the front each pass
questions.explanation: Merge sort recursively splits the array until each piece is trivially sorted (size 1), then merges pairs of sorted pieces back together in order.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of quicksort?
questions.explanation: If the chosen pivot is repeatedly the smallest or largest element, each partition only removes one element, so the algorithm degrades to O(n^2).

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm is most efficient for sorting a nearly-sorted array?
questions.explanation: Insertion sort only moves each element a short distance when the array is nearly sorted, so it approaches O(n) instead of its worst-case O(n^2).

questions.question: Which data structure does BFS use to track nodes to visit?
questions.explanation: BFS explores level by level, so it needs first-in-first-out order: a queue ensures nodes discovered earlier are visited before nodes discovered later.

questions.question: Which data structure does DFS use when implemented iteratively?
questions.explanation: DFS dives as deep as possible before backtracking, which is naturally last-in-first-out: a stack lets you resume the most recently discovered branch first.

questions.question: BFS on an unweighted graph is guaranteed to find which of the following?
answers: The shortest path between two nodes
The deepest node in the graph
questions.explanation: Because BFS visits nodes in order of increasing distance from the start, the first time it reaches any node is guaranteed to be via a shortest path, when every edge has equal weight.

questions.question: Given a tree where the root has two children A and B, A has children C and D, and B has child E. What is the BFS traversal order starting from root?
answers: Root, A, B, C, D, E
Root, A, C, D, B, E
Root, B, E, A, C, D
Root, A, B, E, C, D
questions.explanation: BFS finishes the current depth before moving deeper: root first, then both of its children (A, B), then all of their children (C, D, E).

questions.question: For the same tree (root -> A, B; A -> C, D; B -> E), what is a valid DFS pre-order traversal?
answers: Root, A, C, D, B, E
Root, A, B, C, D, E
C, D, A, E, B, Root
Root, B, E, A, C, D
questions.explanation: Pre-order DFS visits a node, then fully explores its first child's subtree before moving to the next sibling: Root, then all of A's subtree (A, C, D), then all of B's subtree (B, E).

questions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n elements?
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the remaining search space with every comparison, so it takes roughly log2(n) steps to narrow down to one element.

questions.question: An algorithm with two nested loops each iterating over n elements has what time complexity?
questions.explanation: The inner loop runs n times for each of the n iterations of the outer loop, giving n times n, which is O(n^2) total operations.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of bubble sort?
questions.explanation: In the worst case, a reverse-sorted array, bubble sort needs roughly n passes, each comparing up to n elements, giving O(n^2).

questions.question: Which of these time complexities is the most efficient for large values of n?
questions.explanation: O(log n) grows the slowest of the options as n increases. Doubling n only adds one more step, unlike O(n) or O(n^2) which grow much faster.

questions.question: A recursive function calls itself once per element and does O(1) work each call. What is its time complexity?
questions.explanation: One call per element with constant work per call means the total work scales linearly with the number of elements: n calls times O(1) equals O(n).

questions.question: How many usable host addresses does a /29 subnet provide?
questions.explanation: A /29 leaves 3 host bits (32 minus 29), giving 2^3 = 8 total addresses. Subtract the network address and the broadcast address, leaving 6 usable hosts.

questions.question: A subnet uses the mask 255.255.255.192. What is the equivalent CIDR prefix?
A department needs exactly 60 usable IP addresses. What is the smallest CIDR subnet that satisfies this?
questions.explanation: A /26 gives 2^6 minus 2 = 62 usable addresses, the smallest standard subnet that fits 60 hosts. A /27 only gives 30, which is too few.

questions.question: You need subnets that each support 30 hosts from the network 192.168.10.0/24. Which prefix should you use?
questions.explanation: A /27 leaves 5 host bits, giving 2^5 minus 2 = 30 usable addresses, exactly enough for 30 hosts.

questions.question: A VLSM allocation on 10.0.0.0/24 needs a subnet for 100 hosts. Which prefix is the most efficient choice?
questions.explanation: A /25 gives 2^7 minus 2 = 126 usable addresses, the smallest subnet within a /24 that still fits 100 hosts. A /26 only gives 62, which is too small.

questions.question: In Round Robin CPU scheduling, what determines how long each process runs before being preempted?
answers: The number of threads in the process
questions.explanation: Round Robin gives every process a fixed slice of CPU time called the time quantum. When it expires, the OS preempts the process and moves to the next one in the queue.

questions.question: What does throughput measure in the context of CPU scheduling?
answers: CPU utilisation (% of time not idle)
Processes completed per unit of time
Time from process creation to first execution
Time spent waiting in the ready queue
questions.explanation: Throughput is a rate: how many processes the system finishes over a given period. That's different from how responsive or fair the scheduling feels to any single process.

questions.question: What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling?
answers: Preemptive only works on multi-core CPUs
Only non-preemptive can interrupt a running process
Only preemptive can interrupt a running process
They behave identically but differ in implementation
questions.explanation: Preemptive scheduling can forcibly pause a running process to give the CPU to another one, for example when its time quantum ends. Non-preemptive scheduling always lets the running process finish or block on its own first.

questions.question: Which CPU scheduling algorithm can cause starvation for low-priority processes?
answers: Shortest Job First with equal priorities
questions.explanation: If higher-priority processes keep arriving, a strict priority scheduler can keep pushing a low-priority process to the back indefinitely, so it never gets CPU time.

questions.question: What is the main disadvantage of First Come First Served (FCFS) scheduling?
answers: Requires knowing burst time of each process in advance
It can cause starvation of long processes
Long processes block shorter ones, raising average wait time
It does not support multiple CPU cores
questions.explanation: FCFS runs processes strictly in arrival order, so a short process stuck behind a long one has to wait for the entire long process to finish, known as the convoy effect.

questions.question: What is the average-case time complexity of a lookup in a hash table?
questions.explanation: A good hash function spreads keys evenly across buckets, so on average you land close to the right bucket directly instead of searching through many entries.

questions.question: What is a hash collision?
answers: When a hash function returns a negative value
When the table is full and cannot accept more entries
When two different keys produce the same hash index
When a key is not found in the table
questions.explanation: Since a hash table has far fewer buckets than possible keys, two different keys can hash to the same index. That is a collision, and the table needs a strategy to handle it.

questions.question: What does the load factor of a hash table measure?
answers: The number of collisions that have occurred
The ratio of stored entries to total buckets
The maximum chain length under separate chaining
questions.explanation: Load factor equals entries stored divided by number of buckets. As it climbs toward 1 or beyond, collisions become more likely, which is why tables resize when it gets too high.

questions.question: Which collision resolution strategy stores multiple entries at the same index using a linked list?
questions.explanation: Separate chaining keeps a small linked list at each bucket, so when a collision happens the new entry is simply appended to that bucket's chain.

questions.question: In open addressing, what happens when a collision occurs during insertion?
answers: A linked list is created at that index
Another slot in the table is probed for insertion
questions.explanation: Open addressing has no per-bucket list. If a slot is taken, it follows a probing sequence, such as linear or quadratic probing, to find the next open slot in the same table.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of inserting a new node at the head of a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: Inserting at the head just means creating a new node and pointing it at the current head. No traversal is needed regardless of list length.

questions.question: What extra field does a doubly linked list node have compared to a singly linked list node?
answers: A pointer to the tail of the list
A pointer to the previous node
questions.explanation: A singly linked list only points forward with a next pointer. A doubly linked list adds a previous pointer so you can also traverse backward.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of finding the k-th element in a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: Unlike an array, a linked list has no direct addressing. You have to walk from the head one node at a time until you reach the k-th node.

questions.question: Which of the following operations is faster in a linked list than in an array?
answers: Insertion at a known position given a pointer
questions.explanation: If you already hold a pointer to the right spot, inserting into a linked list is just rewiring a couple of pointers in O(1). An array would need to shift every element after that position.

questions.question: Given a direct pointer to a node in a doubly linked list, what is the time complexity of deleting that node?
questions.explanation: With a doubly linked list you can reach both the previous and next node directly through the node's own pointers, so unlinking it takes constant time with no traversal needed.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of reversing a singly linked list in-place?
questions.explanation: Reversing means visiting every node once to flip its next pointer, so the work scales linearly with the number of nodes.

questions.question: What does 'collateral damage' mean in the context of firewall rules?
answers: Rules that accidentally allow malicious traffic through
Rules that block legitimate services sharing a port with the attacker
Rules that exceed the firewall's processing capacity
Outbound packets that bypass the rule set entirely
questions.explanation: If you block an entire port or IP to stop an attacker, you might also block legitimate traffic that happens to share that port or address. That unintended side effect is the collateral damage.

questions.question: An attacker spoofs a legitimate client IP in their packets. Which firewall rule strategy can still block the attack?
questions.explanation: Since the source IP is faked and cannot be trusted, the rule needs to match something the attacker cannot spoof, like the malicious payload itself, combined with the destination port it targets.

questions.question: A firewall uses first-match-wins evaluation. You add 'ALLOW dst_port:4444' before 'DENY dst_port:4444'. What happens to malicious traffic on port 4444?
answers: Both rules apply and the DENY wins
The ALLOW fires first -- malicious traffic passes through
The DENY fires first -- malicious traffic is blocked
The rules cancel each other out
questions.explanation: In first-match-wins evaluation, the firewall stops checking as soon as it finds a matching rule. The earlier ALLOW rule wins, so the later DENY rule never gets evaluated for that traffic.

questions.question: A C2 beacon uses DNS tunnelling over UDP port 53. A legitimate DNS resolver also uses UDP port 53. Which rule blocks ONLY the C2 traffic?
questions.explanation: Blocking all of UDP port 53 would also break legitimate DNS, so the rule needs extra, specific fields, the known malicious source range and the payload signature, to isolate just the malicious traffic.

questions.question: In a multi-channel C2 scenario, all C2 source IPs are spoofed from the 10.0.1.0/24 range but so are legitimate clients. What additional fields should a DENY rule use to avoid false positives?
questions.explanation: Since the source IP range is shared between attacker and legitimate clients, matching on source IP alone would block innocent traffic too. Combining destination port with a payload signature narrows the match to the actual malicious pattern.

questions.question: Which port does HTTP use by default?
questions.explanation: Port 80 is the standard, IANA-assigned default for unencrypted HTTP traffic.

questions.question: A web server accepts encrypted HTTPS connections. Which port does it listen on by default?
questions.explanation: Port 443 is the standard port for HTTPS, which is HTTP wrapped in TLS/SSL encryption.

questions.question: You need to securely log in to a remote Linux server from the command line. Which port must be open on the server?
questions.explanation: SSH, the standard protocol for encrypted remote command-line access, listens on port 22 by default.

questions.question: An old network device uses Telnet. Why is Telnet considered insecure compared to SSH?
answers: Telnet uses a higher port number which is easier to block
Telnet transmits data in plaintext with no encryption
Telnet requires a password but SSH does not
Telnet is slower because it uses port 23 instead of 22
questions.explanation: Telnet sends everything, including usernames and passwords, as plain unencrypted text, so anyone monitoring the network can read it. SSH encrypts the entire session.

questions.question: A mail server sends outgoing email to other servers. Which protocol and port does it use for this?
questions.explanation: SMTP on port 25 is used for server-to-server mail delivery. POP3 and IMAP are instead used by a mail client to retrieve mail, not send it.

questions.question: What is a process in an operating system?
answers: A sequence of instructions stored on disk
A program in execution with its own memory space
A shared memory region between two programs
A function call within a running program
questions.explanation: A program on disk is just static instructions. Once the OS loads it and gives it its own memory space, registers, and execution state, it becomes a running process.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a process and a thread?
answers: Threads have separate memory; processes share memory
Processes have separate memory; threads share it
Threads can only run on a single CPU core
Processes are faster to create than threads
questions.explanation: Each process gets its own isolated memory space. Threads are lighter-weight execution units that live inside a process and share that same memory space with each other.

questions.question: What does context switching refer to in an operating system?
answers: Saving and restoring CPU state between processes or threads
Transferring data between RAM and disk
questions.explanation: To let multiple processes share one CPU, the OS saves the current process's registers and program counter, then loads another's. That save-and-restore is a context switch.

questions.question: What does it mean for a process to be in the blocked state?
answers: It has been terminated by the OS
It is actively running on the CPU
It is waiting for an event such as I/O completion
It has been swapped out to disk
questions.explanation: A blocked process cannot proceed until something external happens, most commonly waiting for disk, network, or user input, so the OS sets it aside and runs something else meanwhile.

questions.question: Which of the following is shared between all threads in the same process?
questions.explanation: Threads in the same process share the heap and other process-wide resources, but each thread keeps its own stack, program counter, and register set so it can execute independently.

questions.question: What is a race condition?
answers: A performance benchmark comparing two algorithms
A bug where two threads compete to finish first
Output that varies based on the ordering of concurrent operations
A deadlock between two processes waiting on each other
questions.explanation: When multiple threads access shared data without proper coordination, the final result can depend on the unpredictable order in which their operations happen to interleave.

questions.question: Which data structure follows Last In First Out (LIFO) ordering?
questions.explanation: LIFO means the most recently added item is the first one removed, exactly like a stack of plates: you take from the top, the last one placed.

questions.question: Which data structure is most appropriate for implementing Breadth First Search (BFS)?
questions.explanation: BFS needs to process discovered nodes in the order they were found, which is first-in-first-out behaviour, exactly what a queue provides.

questions.question: What is a stack overflow in the context of a call stack?
answers: Writing past the end of an array on the heap
Exhausting the call stack from too many nested or recursive calls
A queue becoming larger than its allocated buffer
An integer exceeding its maximum value
questions.explanation: Each function call reserves a small block of memory on the call stack. If calls nest too deeply, often from recursion with no proper base case, the stack runs out of reserved space and crashes.

questions.question: Which data structure would you use to implement an undo feature in a text editor?
questions.explanation: Undo needs to reverse the most recent action first, then the one before that. That is last-in-first-out behaviour, a natural fit for a stack of past actions.

questions.question: A printer receives jobs from multiple users. Which data structure ensures jobs are printed in the order they were submitted?
questions.explanation: Printing jobs in the order they arrive is first-in-first-out behaviour, exactly what a queue guarantees.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of push and pop operations on a stack implemented with a dynamic array?
questions.explanation: Push and pop normally just adjust one end of the array in O(1). Occasionally push triggers a resize that copies everything, but that cost is spread out, or amortised, over many pushes, so the average stays O(1).

questions.question: What property must every node in a BST satisfy?
answers: Its value is greater than all other nodes in the tree
Left descendants are smaller, right descendants are greater
The left and right subtrees must have equal height
Each node must have exactly two children
questions.explanation: The binary search tree ordering rule, every node's left subtree holds smaller values and its right subtree holds larger values, is what makes searching by comparison possible.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of searching in a balanced Binary Search Tree?
questions.explanation: A balanced tree's height is roughly log2(n), and each comparison during search eliminates one whole subtree, so search time scales with the tree's height.

questions.question: In a Binary Search Tree, where is the smallest value always located?
questions.explanation: Because every left child is smaller than its parent, following left pointers as far as possible always leads to the smallest value in the tree.

questions.question: Which tree traversal visits nodes in sorted ascending order when applied to a BST?
questions.explanation: In-order traversal visits left subtree, then the node itself, then right subtree. Since left is always smaller and right is always larger, this visits every value in ascending order.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of insertion into an unbalanced BST?
questions.explanation: If the tree is unbalanced, for example values inserted in already-sorted order, it degenerates into a straight line, so inserting a new node can require walking all n existing nodes.
